summary: This Best Current Practice describes how the IAB sets up and maintains liaison relationships between the IETF and other standards bodies, consortia and industry forums. It also covers appointing liaison managers and representatives and what is expected of them.

plainLanguage.summary: The IETF works with other standards bodies, and this RFC sets out how those working relationships are set up and who is responsible for them. The IAB appoints a liaison manager for each relationship, and no message can be sent in the IETF's name without the right IETF leader agreeing to it first.

questions: how does the iab manage liaison relationships
what is an ietf liaison manager
subtitle: How the IETF's governing board opens, runs and approves working relationships with other standards bodies.

tldr.problem: The IETF is one of several standards development organizations, and it needs formal working relationships with the others so that work is not duplicated and dependencies are known.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB appoints an IETF liaison manager for each relationship, keeps the relationship informal where possible, and requires an explicit approval from the relevant IETF body before any liaison statement is sent.
tldr.outcome: The result is a Best Current Practice, BCP 102, that tells both sides who speaks for the IETF and who signs off on a message leaving the community.

facts.label: Out of scope
facts.value: Managing other organizations' liaison managers to the IETF

today: RFC 4052 is a Best Current Practice, BCP 102, and has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the description of how the IAB opens, runs and approves IETF liaison relationships. The procedures for sending and answering liaison statements themselves live in a separate document, which this RFC points to rather than restates.

sections.title: Liaison Relationships and Personnel
sections.content:
The IETF, as an organization, needs to engage in direct communication or joint endeavours with various other formal organizations. The IETF is one of several Standards Development Organizations, or SDOs, and all SDOs find it increasingly necessary to communicate and coordinate activities involving Internet-related technologies. That is useful in order to avoid overlap in work efforts and to manage interactions between their groups. Where mutual effort to communicate and coordinate is formalised, these relationships are generically referred to as liaison relationships.

For each relationship a person from the IETF is designated to manage it, and that person is generally called the IETF liaison manager to the other organization. When the relationship is expected to encompass a complex or broad range of activities, more people may be designated to undertake some portions of the communications, coordinated by the liaison manager. Often the other organization designates its own liaison manager to the IETF in return.

The document is chiefly concerned with the establishment and maintenance of liaison relationships and with the appointment and responsibilities of IETF liaison managers and representatives. The management of other organizations' liaison managers to the IETF is outside its scope. The IETF has chartered the Internet Architecture Board (IAB) to manage liaison relationships, and consistent with its charter the IAB acts as representative of the interests of the IETF and the Internet Society in technical liaison relationships. Liaison relationships are kept as informal as possible and must be of demonstrable value to the IETF's technical mandate.

A liaison relationship is most valuable when there are areas of technical development of mutual interest, because SDOs would rather leverage existing work done by other organizations than recreate it themselves. Establishing one can prevent inadvertent duplication of effort, without obstructing either organization from pursuing its own mandate, and can provide authoritative information of one organization's dependencies on the other's work.
sections.plainLanguage: A liaison relationship is a formal way for the IETF and another standards body to work together without repeating each other's work. The IAB keeps these relationships, and each one has an IETF liaison manager who looks after day-to-day communication.

sections.title: Setting Up a Liaison Relationship
sections.content:
A liaison relationship is set up when it is mutually agreeable and needed for some specific purpose, in the view of the other organization, the IAB, and the IETF participants conducting the work. There is no set process or form for this. The IETF participants and the peer organization approach the IAB, and after discussion come to an agreement to form the relationship. In some cases the intended scope and guidelines for the collaboration are documented specifically.

In setting up the relationship, the IAB expects a mutual exchange of views and discussion of the best approach for undertaking new standardization work items. Any work items resulting for the IETF will be undertaken in the usual IETF procedures. The peer organization often has a different organizational structure and procedures from the IETF, which will require some flexibility on the part of both organizations to accommodate. The IAB expects that each organization will use the relationship carefully, allowing time for the processes it requests to occur in the other organization, and will not make unreasonable demands.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no form to fill in. The people doing the work and the peer body approach the IAB, talk it over, and agree a relationship. From then on the IETF still does its own work by its own rules, and each side gives the other time to work in its own way.

sections.title: The Liaison Manager
sections.content:
Most work on mutually interesting topics will be carried out in the usual way within the IETF and the peer organization, so most communications will be informal in nature, for example Working Group or mailing list discussions. An important function of the liaison manager is to ensure that communication is maintained, productive, and timely. The liaison manager may use any applicable businesslike approach, from private to public communications, and bring in other parties as needed.

If a communication from a peer organization is addressed to an inappropriate party, such as being sent to the Working Group but not copying the Area Director, or being sent to the wrong Working Group, the liaison manager will help redirect or otherwise augment the communication. Liaison managers should also communicate and coordinate with other liaison managers where concerned technical activities overlap.

Since the IAB is ultimately responsible for liaison relationships, anyone who has a problem with a relationship, whether an IETF participant or a person from the peer organization, should first consult the IAB's designated liaison manager, and if that does not result in a satisfactory outcome, the IAB itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The liaison manager keeps the conversation going and on time. If a message from the other body arrives at the wrong group, the liaison manager puts it right. Anyone unhappy with how a relationship is working goes to the liaison manager first and to the IAB if that does not settle it.

sections.title: Liaison Representatives
sections.content:
The liaison manager is, specifically, a representative of the IETF for the purpose of managing the liaison relationship. There may be occasion to identify other representatives for the same relationship. For example, if the area of mutual work is extensive it might be appropriate to name several people as liaison representatives to different parts of the other organization. Or it might be appropriate to name a liaison representative to attend a particular meeting.

These other liaison representatives are selected by the IAB and work in conjunction, and close communication, with the liaison manager. In some cases this may also require communication and coordination with other liaison managers or representatives where concerned technical activities overlap. The specific responsibilities of the liaison representative will be identified at the time of appointment.
sections.plainLanguage: A relationship that covers a lot of ground may need more than one person. The IAB can name extra liaison representatives for parts of the other organization or for a single meeting. They are appointed for a stated job and work closely with the liaison manager.

sections.title: Liaison Communications
sections.content: Communications between organizations use a variety of formal and informal channels. The stated preference of the IETF, which is largely an informal organization, is to use informal channels, as these have historically worked well to expedite matters. In some cases, however, a more formal communication is appropriate, either as an adjunct to the informal channel or in its place. In the case of formal communications, the established procedures of many organizations use a form known as a liaison statement. Procedures for sending, managing, and responding to liaison statements are discussed in a separate document.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF prefers informal channels such as working group discussions, because they get things done quickly. When a formal note is needed, the usual form is a liaison statement, which is a document one standards body sends to another.

sections.title: Liaison Manager Responsibilities
sections.content:
The requirements vary with the nature of the peer organization and the type of joint work being undertaken, but the general expectations of a liaison manager appointed by the IAB are as follows.

  • Attend relevant meetings of the peer organization as needed and report back to the appropriate IETF organization any material updates.
  • Carry any messages from the IETF to the peer organization when specifically instructed. Generally these communications represent the IETF, so due care and consensus must be applied in their construction.
  • Prepare occasional updates. The target of these updates, for example the IAB, an Area Director or a Working Group, will generally be identified upon appointment.
  • Oversee delivery of liaison statements addressed to the IETF, ensuring that they reach the appropriate destination within the IETF, and ensure that relevant responses from the IETF are created and sent in a timely fashion.
  • Work with the other organization to ensure that the IETF's liaison statements are appropriately directed and responded to in a timely fashion.
  • Communicate and coordinate with other IETF liaison managers and representatives where concerned technical activities overlap.
sections.plainLanguage: The liaison manager attends the other body's meetings and reports back, carries messages when told to, writes occasional updates, makes sure statements arriving for the IETF reach the right group and get an answer, and keeps other liaison managers in step where the work overlaps.

sections.title: Approving and Sending Liaison Statements
sections.content:
It is important that appropriate leadership review be made of proposed IETF liaison statements, and that those writing such statements, who claim to be speaking on behalf of the IETF, are truly representing IETF views. All outgoing liaison statements will be copied to the IETF Secretariat using the procedures defined in the separate liaison statement document or its successors.

For a liaison statement generated on behalf of an IETF Working Group, the Working Group chairs must create a statement based on appropriate discussions within the group to ensure working group consensus for the positions presented. The chairs must have generated or must agree with the sending of the statement, and must advise the Area Directors that it has been sent by copying them on the message.

For a statement generated on behalf of an IETF Area, the Area Directors must have generated or must agree with the sending. If it is not sent by the Area Directors, their agreement must be obtained in advance and confirmed by copying them on the message. For a statement generated on behalf of the IETF as a whole, the IETF Chair must have generated or must agree with the sending, with the same rule for prior agreement. For a statement generated by the IAB, the IAB Chair must have generated or must agree with the sending, again with the same rule.

In cases where prior agreement was not obtained, and the designated authority in fact does not agree with the message, that authority will work with the liaison manager to follow up as appropriate, including emitting a revised liaison statement if necessary. The RFC calls this a situation best avoided by assuring appropriate agreement in advance of sending the liaison message.
sections.plainLanguage: A statement only speaks for the IETF if the right IETF leader agrees to it. Working group statements need the group chairs, area statements need the Area Directors, statements for the whole IETF need the IETF Chair, and statements from the IAB need the IAB Chair.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC states the position in one line: the security of the Internet is not threatened by these procedures. The document governs how people talk to each other across standards bodies, not how packets are built or sent, so it introduces no protocol behaviour that could weaken the Internet's security.
sections.plainLanguage: These procedures do not affect the security of the Internet. They are about how people talk to each other, not about how data is sent.

viz.caption: THE IETF BODIES NAMED IN RFC 4052

children.label: Working Group
children.note: Chairs create statements on behalf of the group.

children.label: Area
children.note: Area Directors agree to statements on behalf of the area.

children.label: IETF Chair
children.note: Agrees to statements on behalf of the IETF as a whole.

children.label: IAB
children.note: Manages liaison relationships; the IAB Chair agrees to statements the IAB generates.

viz.caption: WHAT THE IAB EXPECTS OF A LIAISON MANAGER

items.title: Attend and report
items.text: Go to the peer organization's meetings when needed and report material updates back to the IETF.

items.title: Carry messages
items.text: Pass messages from the IETF to the peer organization when instructed, with care and consensus.

items.title: Prepare updates
items.text: Write occasional updates for the target named at appointment, such as the IAB, an Area Director or a Working Group.

items.title: Receive statements
items.text: Make sure incoming statements reach the right IETF destination and get a timely response.

items.title: Send statements
items.text: Work with the other organization so that IETF statements are directed properly and answered in time.

items.title: Coordinate
items.text: Coordinate with other IETF liaison managers and representatives where the technical work overlaps.
